analysis.one_liner: Set a national energy strategy to curb greenhouse gases through efficiency standards, renewable and alternative fuel research, and federal building upgrades.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed a heavily rewritten version by voice vote on August 4, 1990, but the House never voted, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set national goals for stabilizing greenhouse gas emissions and required a least-cost national energy strategy, a climate office at the Energy Department, energy ratings for homes, labels for windows, conservation upgrades in federal buildings, and research funding for solar, wind, hydrogen, fuel cells, electric vehicles, and natural gas. The version Senator Tim Wirth introduced in 1989 went further: it required cutting carbon dioxide 20 percent below 1988 levels by 2000. Before the Senate voted, that binding target was replaced with a study of whether such a cut was feasible, and the Senate passed the softened version by voice vote. The House never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households would have gotten energy-efficiency ratings for homes, labels for windows, and lower long-term energy costs as utilities were pushed to treat conservation as an investment equal to building new power plants. Federal taxpayers would have saved through required upgrades to federal buildings. Renewable energy, hydrogen, fuel cell, electric vehicle, and natural gas industries would have gained research funding, joint ventures, and expanded market access under federal power rules.

how_it_helps.text: Required every future National Energy Policy Plan to include a least-cost energy strategy aimed at stabilizing and eventually reducing U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, with efficiency given priority when its cost equaled that of new energy supply.

Created a Director of Climate Protection at the Department of Energy and commissioned independent National Academies reviews of climate science and policy options, with reports sent to Congress without administration clearance.

Required federal agencies to install all energy conservation measures with payback periods under ten years in federal buildings by 2000, with funding penalties for agencies that lagged, and directed the development of home energy-efficiency ratings and window labels for buyers.

Amended utility law so that investments in conservation and efficiency would be as profitable for electric utilities as building new generation plants, and removed for two years the size limits that kept larger solar, wind, waste, and geothermal plants out of favorable federal treatment.

Authorized research, development, and demonstration funding for renewable energy, hydrogen production, fuel cells, electric vehicles, natural gas vehicles, and clean coal technologies for fiscal years 1992 through 1994.

The original introduced version went further: it set a binding national goal of cutting carbon dioxide at least 20 percent below 1988 levels by 2000 and repealed the mandatory below-cost timber program in Alaska's Tongass National Forest.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and electric utilities would have borne the main costs, from efficiency requirements and conservation mandates that reduce power sales to the emissions goals that threatened demand for coal and oil. Taxpayers would have funded the research programs, federal building upgrades, and weatherization assistance.

drawbacks.text: Even the Senate-passed version contained no binding emission limits — the 20 percent cut below 1988 levels by 2000 in the introduced bill became a study of the feasibility of a 20 percent cut by 2005 — so the bill as passed would have produced mostly reports, studies, and modest research money.

A binding carbon dioxide reduction target, as in the original bill, could have raised energy prices and cost jobs in coal and oil regions; the Departments of Energy, Transportation, and the Interior and NASA all submitted unfavorable comments on the bill during committee review.

Some provisions directed federal research money toward specific established industries, including clean coal, natural gas recovery, and an advanced nuclear reactor study, which public-interest critics would call corporate subsidy rather than climate policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: As introduced, this was a serious climate and efficiency bill whose costs would have fallen mainly on fossil energy producers while savings accrued to energy consumers. By the time the Senate passed it, the binding target was gone and the Tongass timber reform was gone, leaving a bill of studies, modest R&D authorizations, and worthwhile but limited efficiency measures — helpful at the margins, unlikely to change emission trends on its own.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed a much-watered-down version by voice vote in August 1990, but the House committees it was sent to never reported it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Wirth introduced the bill in February 1989 with a binding goal of cutting U.S. carbon dioxide emissions at least 20 percent below 1988 levels by 2000 and a demand for an international climate convention by 1992.

The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee held hearings through 1989 and 1990; the Departments of Energy, Transportation, and the Interior and NASA each submitted unfavorable executive comments.

The committee reported the bill on July 11, 1990 with an amendment in the nature of a substitute that replaced the binding 20-percent-by-2000 goal with a goal of merely investigating the feasibility of stabilizing or cutting emissions by 2005, and dropped the Tongass timber reform.
The Senate passed the rewritten bill by voice vote on August 4, 1990, with no recorded vote.

The House received the bill on September 5, 1990, referred it jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Science, Space and Technology Committees, and sent it to the Energy and Power Subcommittee on September 24; neither committee ever reported it, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
The action history notes the bill was related to H.R. 5835, the House's vehicle for energy legislation that Congress, suggesting the House addressed the subject through its own bill instead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and electric utilities avoided the binding carbon dioxide cuts and conservation mandates the original bill proposed, and Alaska timber interests kept the Tongass arrangement after that provision was stripped. The House committees that never acted preserved the status quo.

for.name: Sen. Tim Wirth
for.role: U.S. Senator from Colorado; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with a binding 20 percent carbon dioxide reduction goal and drove it through committee hearings over two years.

for.name: Sen. Bennett Johnston
for.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the Senate with a substitute amendment on July 11, 1990, and it passed the Senate by voice vote on August 4, 1990.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the Senate-passed bill on September 5, 1990, referred it to the Energy and Power Subcommittee on September 24, and never reported it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Executive branch agencies (Energy, Transportation, Interior, NASA)
against.what_they_did: Each submitted unfavorable executive comments to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee during 1989 and 1990.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory greenhouse gas reduction targets during this period; his administration favored voluntary approaches and resisted binding emissions goals.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 33 of 55 Senate Democrats and 7 of 45 Senate Republicans cosponsored, and the Senate passed the bill by voice vote with no recorded opposition; it died through House committee inaction, not a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required utilities to make conservation investments as profitable as building new power plants, cutting into electricity sales growth, while also funding fuel cell and natural gas demonstrations and easing rules for some renewable generators. Utilities historically resisted demand-side mandates because revenue depends on selling more power.

The bill set a national goal of stabilizing carbon dioxide emissions, which threatens coal demand, but also funded clean coal research, carbon dioxide capture studies, and non-fuel coal products. The industry gains research dollars while the policy goal runs against its core business.

industries.industry: Renewable energy industries (solar, wind, geothermal, biomass)
industries.note: The bill authorized research and joint venture funding, and removed for two years the size limits that excluded larger solar, wind, waste, and geothermal plants from favorable federal power-purchase rules. These industries' growth depends on the same emission reductions the public wants.

The bill funded natural gas vehicles, transit conversions, recovery research, heating technology, and agreements with the Gas Research Institute. Gas benefited as a lower-carbon substitute for coal and oil, which tracks the public interest in emissions reduction, though not as directly as renewables.

The introduced bill would have repealed the mandatory annual appropriations for Tongass timber sales — a program that sold federal old-growth timber below cost — and imposed a harvest moratorium; that provision was dropped before Senate passage, leaving the industry's subsidized arrangement intact. The industry's profits in that arrangement came from below-cost federal sales at taxpayer expense.
